candidate.title: Cross-domain calibration and selective prediction for crop-disease AI
candidate.workingTitle: Evaluating Calibration and Selective Prediction for Crop-Disease Recognition Under Geographic and Acquisition Shift
candidate.summary: Can crop-disease models retain reliable confidence and useful selective prediction when evaluated across independently sourced field domains with different acquisition conditions and geography?
candidate.shortDescription: A reliability-centred experimental study of confidence calibration and selective prediction under acquisition/geographic shift, using leakage-resistant evaluation as a methodological control.
candidate.ghanaianRelevance: Field agriculture in Ghana is a possible setting, not a requirement. Public datasets are preferred unless local images can be collected properly.
candidate.technicalContribution: A reproducible cross-domain evaluation protocol and comparative analysis of calibration and selective-prediction behaviour under documented acquisition/geographic shift. The contribution is not another disease classifier and does not assume that calibration on one benchmark transfers to other domains.

feasibility.rationale: This is a planning assessment. The work is measurable if a public dataset's provenance and split metadata can be audited.

candidate.dataRequirements: Candidate sources now include PaddyDoctor (16,225 rice field images, 13 classes); Ghana CCMT (24,881 raw images across cashew, cassava, maize and tomato, plus 102,976 augmented images across 22 classes); PlantVillage, Cassava, Tomato, PlantDoc and other field-oriented datasets. PALM-Net, EffiToRag, ARTEN and SAGE use different datasets and tasks. Gookyi et al. (2026) provide Ghanaian multi-modal cowpea/maize field-trial data and field photographs, but the published description does not identify disease labels; do not treat it as a supervised disease-recognition benchmark. Verify licensing, original-image provenance, source/plant/session/farm metadata, class compatibility and whether external domains are genuinely independent before selecting data.
candidate.evaluationDesign: Use one bounded crop/disease task and a small number of independently sourced domains. Establish leakage-resistant splits at the strongest defensible grouping level (original image, plant, session, farm or source) before model evaluation; keep augmented derivatives with their source image and never treat them as independent observations. Compare calibration methods and selective-prediction strategies under in-domain and cross-domain evaluation. Report discrimination (e.g. macro-F1), calibration (ECE with documented binning, Brier score, NLL), selective risk/coverage (including AURC where appropriate), and degradation under defined acquisition/geographic shifts. Include conventional model baselines; a VLM may be included only if it serves the fixed reliability question. Separate corruption testing from genuine external-domain validation.
majorRisks: Recent work already evaluates calibration, deduplication, corruption robustness, multi-dataset field performance, and knowledge-grounded diagnosis. The thesis must not claim that these dimensions have never been studied.
A single PaddyDoctor corpus, even with deduplication and corruption tests, does not establish generalisation across geography, season, device, or independently collected datasets.
Public datasets differ in crop, disease taxonomy, labels, collection conditions and licensing; cross-dataset evaluation may require a carefully defined common label subset or a single-crop scope.
CCMT raw and augmented image counts are now supported by its data paper, but source-level duplicate relationships and split leakage still require an audit; do not assume overlap without testing.
Gookyi et al. (2026) is a Ghanaian field-trial dataset, not a disease-labelled benchmark in the available dataset description.
Adding multiple crops, Ghanaian field collection, VLMs, explainability, RAG, and a new classifier simultaneously would exceed a focused one-year MPhil.
openDecisions: Which one crop/disease task and which two or three independently sourced domains provide genuinely different acquisition/geographic conditions?
Which datasets expose enough provenance to construct defensible plant/session/farm/source-disjoint splits?
What is the primary external-shift definition: acquisition device/lighting, geography, season, or a carefully chosen combination?
Which calibration and selective-prediction methods can be compared fairly with the available calibration data?
Will a conventional vision model be the primary test system, with a VLM retained only as an optional secondary comparison?

nodes.title: High crop-disease benchmark performance may not transfer across field domains
nodes.summary: Strong results on one curated or deduplicated dataset do not establish reliable confidence on independently sourced field images.
nodes.detail: The recent literature review materially narrows the problem. A PaddyDoctor study already combines a deduplicated split, post-hoc calibration, risk/coverage analysis and corruption testing. PALM-Net evaluates multiple datasets and claims field robustness; EffiToRag combines image diagnosis with knowledge retrieval; ARTEN publishes enhanced derivatives of an existing image collection; and SAGE explores source-grounded, agentic diagnosis at much larger scale. The thesis must therefore not frame calibration or field robustness as wholly unexplored. The remaining question to test is whether calibrated confidence and selective prediction remain reliable across independently sourced domains with different acquisition and geographic conditions. Dataset leakage control remains essential experimental hygiene, not necessarily the sole novelty claim. The CCMT dataset paper has now been checked for its 24,881 raw and 102,976 augmented image counts; the earlier claim of actual train/test overlap remains unverified and must be established by file-level auditing.
assumptions: A public dataset exists with enough provenance or image similarity structure to test a meaningful split strategy.
Reliability should be evaluated beyond top-line accuracy.
risks: If the dataset does not permit a defensible leakage audit, the contamination component must be narrowed or dropped.

nodes.title: How do calibration and selective prediction behave under cross-domain field acquisition and geographic shift?
nodes.summary: How reliably do model confidence and selective risk transfer across independently sourced crop-disease field domains when splits prevent source leakage?
nodes.detail: The central question is now external-domain reliability: whether calibration and selective-prediction methods remain useful when a model moves between independently sourced datasets or field domains with different acquisition conditions and geography. Leakage-resistant splitting is a necessary control, informed by prior dataset contamination concerns. The recent PaddyDoctor paper means calibration on a single dataset is not itself a novelty claim. The thesis should measure cross-domain calibration and risk/coverage behaviour, not simply compare classifier accuracy.

nodes.title: Why reliability is the contribution
nodes.summary: The field already has many classifiers. The opening is in how performance is measured.
nodes.detail: The study is relevant to Ghanaian agriculture because model performance in deployment depends on real field conditions, not only curated benchmarks. Ghana-specific images would strengthen contextual relevance but are not mandatory if public datasets support a rigorous experiment. The computing contribution is reliability evaluation for computer-vision systems.

nodes.title: Local field images are optional
nodes.summary: Local field images are optional
nodes.detail: Public datasets are the default. Ghana-specific field photographs may be added only if collection and annotation are feasible. They are not required to state the problem.

nodes.title: An evaluation protocol for vision models
nodes.summary: An evaluation protocol for vision models
nodes.detail: The technical contribution is experimental design and evaluation: data-provenance audit, leakage-aware partitioning, domain-shift construction, calibration analysis, and selective prediction. It is not simply training a new crop classifier.

nodes.title: What would count as a contribution
nodes.summary: What would count as a contribution
nodes.detail: A reproducible protocol and empirical evidence showing how split strategy and field shift change both predictive performance and trustworthiness. The thesis should report uncertainty and coverage-risk trade-offs rather than a single accuracy score.

nodes.title: Calibration and selective prediction
nodes.summary: Calibration and selective prediction

nodes.title: High curated accuracy is a weak deployment claim
nodes.summary: High curated accuracy is a weak deployment claim
nodes.detail: Crop-disease recognition is an established classification field. Recent work includes multi-dataset field-oriented recognition (PALM-Net), calibrated and deduplicated rice diagnosis on PaddyDoctor, knowledge-grounded diagnosis with EfficientNetV2 and RAG (EffiToRag), image enhancement datasets (ARTEN), and agentic visual diagnosis grounded in source-cited symptom knowledge (SAGE). The candidate must distinguish itself through a carefully bounded reliability question and an evaluation protocol, not by proposing another classifier.

nodes.title: Reported test scores may not survive a change of field conditions
nodes.summary: Reported test scores may not survive a change of field conditions
nodes.detail: The recent literature confirms that field variability and cross-dataset performance are already being studied. The narrower hypothesis is that reported robustness or accuracy across selected datasets does not by itself establish calibrated confidence and useful selective prediction under genuinely independent acquisition/geographic shifts. The exact domain definitions and comparable labels must be fixed before claiming a gap.
risks: Do not expand this into explainability, fairness, compression, and diagnosis at once.
validationRequirements: Extract the exact datasets, crops, disease classes, split strategy, and acquisition conditions from each paper.
Identify whether the test set is genuinely external/field-based or merely a different curated dataset.
Avoid claiming a gap if a directly comparable evaluation already exists.

nodes.title: Leakage and correlated splits
nodes.summary: Leakage and correlated splits
nodes.detail: Near-duplicate images, capture sessions, or the same plant appearing on both sides of a split.

nodes.title: Random image splits can leak near-duplicates
nodes.summary: Random image splits can leak near-duplicates
nodes.detail: The project raised the risk that random image-level splits can place near-duplicates or correlated images from the same plant/session/source in both train and test partitions. The recent PaddyDoctor paper reports exact and near-duplicate removal using SHA-256 and perceptual hashing before splitting. CCMT is a Ghanaian dataset paper with 24,881 raw images and a separate 102,976-image augmented collection across 22 classes. The CCMT counts are supported by its data paper; however, the existence and extent of leakage in any chosen split must be measured rather than assumed. Split original images first and keep augmented derivatives with their source.
risks: The proposed leakage analysis depends on actual duplicate/capture metadata or a defensible similarity-based audit.

nodes.title: Random splits may overstate generalisation when images are correlated
nodes.summary: Random splits may overstate generalisation when images are correlated
nodes.detail: A candidate gap is that random image-level splits may overestimate generalisation when images are correlated by plant, session, source, or near-duplicate content. This must be tested against the selected dataset documentation and literature; do not assume a random split is contaminated without evidence. A key rule from the discussions: split original images first and keep augmented versions of an original in the same partition. Augmented copies must never be counted as independent test observations.
validationRequirements: Audit near-duplicates and source/session grouping before selecting split methods.
Report the unit of grouping and justify why it blocks the relevant leakage path.

nodes.detail: Whether accuracy hides overconfident or poorly calibrated predictions when the field distribution changes.

nodes.title: Accuracy does not describe confidence
nodes.summary: Accuracy does not describe confidence
nodes.detail: A recent PaddyDoctor study reports post-hoc temperature scaling and multiple probability-quality metrics. Its reported test ECE increases slightly from 0.82% to 0.94% after scaling, while Brier score and NLL improve slightly. This is a concrete example of calibration trade-offs and shows why the thesis must report more than accuracy or a single ECE value. The study also reports AURC and corruption robustness. Its results are from one rice dataset and do not establish cross-geographic, seasonal or device-level external validity.

nodes.title: Calibration measured on one benchmark may not transfer to independent field domains
nodes.summary: Accuracy can hide unsafe confidence under distribution shift
nodes.detail: The research question is no longer whether crop-disease models can be calibrated at all: a recent PaddyDoctor study explicitly evaluates temperature scaling, ECE, Brier score, NLL and risk/coverage. The unresolved issue for this project is whether calibration and selective-prediction behaviour remain reliable when the evaluation domain changes across independent sources, devices, locations or seasons. This is a candidate gap requiring a systematic comparison of recent studies and a feasible external dataset design; it is not yet an established absence in the literature.
validationRequirements: Select calibration metrics appropriate to the task and report their limitations.
Compare risk/coverage curves or another justified selective-prediction evaluation.

nodes.detail: Conventional image classifiers compared with vision-language approaches, only if the literature justifies it.

nodes.title: Another classifier bake-off is not the contribution
nodes.summary: Another classifier bake-off is not the contribution
nodes.detail: The recent landscape is broader than conventional image classifiers. EffiToRag couples EfficientNetV2 diagnosis to retrieval-grounded agronomic recommendations; SAGE uses a training-free agentic visual reasoning process with source-grounded symptom knowledge; PALM-Net proposes population-aware multilinear feature learning. These are different system designs and should not be treated as directly comparable baselines without matching tasks, data and evaluation protocols. A VLM/agent comparison remains optional, not the core contribution.

nodes.title: It is unknown whether vision-language models change the failure mode
nodes.summary: It is unknown whether vision-language models change the failure mode
nodes.detail: A possible question is whether a selected few-shot vision-language approach changes the pattern of failure, calibration, or selective prediction under the same field shift. This is not yet a confirmed literature gap and may be removed if it expands the study beyond a one-year MPhil. The potential novelty is not simply using a VLM. It is evaluating whether few-shot VLMs maintain calibration and useful selective prediction under cross-domain field shift when the split protocol blocks leakage. Include the VLM only if literature review confirms this question is not already answered and the experiment remains bounded.
validationRequirements: Establish a specific reason to include a VLM from the literature, not novelty-by-model choice.
Use the same data, shift conditions, and evaluation protocol for all compared model families.

nodes.title: External-domain validation and confidence transfer
nodes.summary: What happens to confidence and selective risk when the source domain changes?
nodes.detail: This area isolates the newly narrowed question. It brings together recent calibrated single-corpus work, multi-dataset field-oriented recognition, knowledge-grounded systems and Ghanaian data availability. The central comparison must be between genuinely independent domains, not merely different random partitions of one source collection.

nodes.title: A PaddyDoctor study already evaluates deduplication, calibration and corruption robustness
nodes.summary: A recent rice-disease study reports a leakage-resistant split, calibration trade-offs and strong sensitivity to brightness and blur.
nodes.detail: Singh, Singh and Dhelim evaluate a ResNet-34+CBAM rice-disease model on 16,225 PaddyDoctor field images across 13 classes. The paper reports 95.13% accuracy and 95.14% weighted F1 on its deduplicated test split. Temperature scaling slightly improves Brier score (0.0760 to 0.0758) and NLL (0.1573 to 0.1566), but test ECE rises from 0.82% to 0.94%. The paper also reports severe accuracy drops under brightness shift (47.72%) and Gaussian blur (32.13%). Its stated limitation is the need for evaluation across seasons, devices and geographic regions. These findings directly narrow the proposed thesis: calibration and corruption testing exist, while external-domain calibration transfer remains a defensible question to investigate.

nodes.title: Recent systems address field robustness and knowledge grounding through different methods
nodes.summary: PALM-Net, EffiToRag, ARTEN and SAGE broaden the current status quo, but they do not constitute one directly comparable calibration study.
nodes.detail: PALM-Net evaluates PlantVillage, Cassava and Tomato datasets with a population-aware multilinear network and reports Top-1 accuracies of 99.32%, 84.56% and 97.44%, respectively. EffiToRag combines EfficientNetV2 diagnosis with retrieval-augmented agronomic recommendations and reports results on a held-out CDDM set of 11,621 images and 60 classes. ARTEN is an enhanced derivative of an existing 21,875-image multi-crop collection; its authors state that no new field observations were introduced and that image-quality metrics alone do not establish preservation of disease-specific features. SAGE is an agentic, source-grounded visual diagnosis system and dataset spanning approximately 839,000 images, 335 crops and 1,251 disease classes; its project page reports an average 16.2 percentage-point gain from symptom knowledge at the full reference budget. These systems differ in tasks, data and methods. The thesis should compare only what can be fairly aligned and should not imply that these works all evaluate confidence calibration.

nodes.title: Ghanaian crop datasets differ in their suitability for disease-reliability experiments
nodes.summary: CCMT is disease-labelled Ghanaian image data; the Gookyi field-trial dataset is contextual agricultural data, not a disease-labelled benchmark.
nodes.detail: The CCMT data paper describes 24,881 raw images from cashew, cassava, maize and tomato and a separate augmented collection of 102,976 images across 22 categories. The Gookyi et al. 2026 Mendeley dataset documents a 15-week field trial at Sumbrungu, Bolgatanga, covering six cowpea and maize varieties, soil/environmental variables, irrigation and field photographs. Its published description does not provide disease labels, so it may support contextual understanding of Ghanaian field acquisition but should not be treated as a supervised crop-disease test set without additional verified annotations.

nodes.title: Cross-domain confidence calibration and selective risk remain to be tested under independent acquisition and geographic shift
nodes.summary: The proposed gap concerns transfer of reliability, not the existence of calibration methods.
nodes.detail: The PaddyDoctor study demonstrates calibration and corruption evaluation on one deduplicated rice corpus, while PALM-Net and other recent systems explore multi-dataset or field-oriented diagnosis. The available source material does not establish a common, leakage-resistant comparison of calibration and selective-prediction behaviour across independent geographic/acquisition domains. This is a bounded research hypothesis, not proof that no such study exists. A systematic full-text review must check whether recent papers already perform this exact combination.

nodes.title: Evaluate calibration and selective prediction across independent field domains
nodes.summary: Hold the model protocol fixed and test reliability across a small, defensible set of independent acquisition/geographic domains.
nodes.detail: A focused study could select one crop/disease task and two or three datasets with sufficiently compatible labels and documented provenance. Establish source-disjoint or group-disjoint splits within each source, then evaluate cross-domain transfer, calibration and selective prediction. Avoid making Ghanaian data collection, multiple crop families, RAG, explainability and VLM development all core deliverables.

nodes.title: How do calibration and selective-prediction methods behave across independent crop-disease field domains?
nodes.summary: How do calibration quality and risk-coverage change when evaluation moves across datasets with different acquisition and geographic conditions?
nodes.detail: The experiment should report both in-domain and cross-domain results using the same model and calibration protocol. It should distinguish controlled corruption tests from genuine external-domain evaluation and explain the provenance of each dataset and split.
validationRequirements: Use at least two genuinely independent domains with compatible labels.
Document split grouping, deduplication, calibration data and test data separately.
Report ECE with binning details, Brier score, NLL, risk-coverage/AURC and discrimination metrics.
Do not fit calibration parameters on the external test domain.

evidenceLinks.claim: Project notes report Description-Guided CLIP 16-shot accuracies of 93.16% on PlantVillage, 79.30% on Cassava, and 96.56% on Pear, plus 56.96% on 21-class PlantDoc cross-domain evaluation.
evidenceLinks.limitation: All figures and the exact evaluation protocol need checking against the full paper. Local evidence calibration should not be confused with conventional predictive-confidence calibration.
evidenceLinks.notes: Bibliographic record and the paper's actual findings still need to be checked.

evidenceLinks.claim: AgriPath-LF16 is noted as a possible field-oriented dataset or task.
evidenceLinks.limitation: Composition and split design are unverified.
evidenceLinks.notes: Bibliographic record and the paper's actual findings still need to be checked.

evidenceLinks.claim: Project notes report a Kang (2026) finding that 91.9% of CDD test images share sensor readings with training images.
evidenceLinks.limitation: The exact paper, dataset, definition of sensor-reading overlap, and result have not been verified.
evidenceLinks.notes: Bibliographic record and the paper's actual findings still need to be checked.

evidenceLinks.claim: Project notes report CCMT as having 24,881 original images and 102,976 augmented images across four crops and 22 categories, and raise a concern about related/augmented image overlap across splits.
evidenceLinks.limitation: Counts, dataset version, class distribution, augmentation provenance, and the reported overlap are not verified. The dataset may or may not expose metadata sufficient for group-disjoint splitting.
evidenceLinks.notes: Audit the original release and split construction; never treat augmented images as independent source observations.

evidenceLinks.claim: Project notes describe BLAP as a lead with 990 images, 11 crops, 33 categories, reported 92.78% accuracy, and a 360-image wheat-field evaluation with 36/36 test images reportedly correct.
evidenceLinks.limitation: Dataset composition, metrics, test design, and the exact paper are unverified; the small field test must not be generalised.
evidenceLinks.notes: Bibliographic record and the paper's actual findings still need to be checked.

evidenceLinks.claim: The article reports a deduplicated PaddyDoctor evaluation with post-hoc temperature scaling, ECE, Brier, NLL and corruption analysis.
evidenceLinks.limitation: The evaluation is based on one PaddyDoctor corpus; the paper itself identifies cross-season, cross-device and cross-geographic validation as future work.
evidenceLinks.notes: Abstract and article landing-page content checked; figures are author-reported.

evidenceLinks.claim: PALM-Net reports results on PlantVillage, Cassava and Tomato datasets and is explicitly framed around field robustness.
evidenceLinks.limitation: The available abstract emphasises classification and feature robustness; do not infer calibration/selective-prediction evaluation from it.

evidenceLinks.claim: EffiToRag combines EfficientNetV2 diagnosis with retrieval-grounded agronomic recommendation on a held-out CDDM test set.
evidenceLinks.limitation: Different task from calibration transfer; held-out CDDM performance is not proof of independent external-domain validity.

evidenceLinks.claim: ARTEN publishes enhanced derivatives of an existing 21,875-image multi-crop collection and explicitly states that no new field observations were introduced.
evidenceLinks.limitation: A derived enhanced image collection should not be counted as an independent field domain; image-quality metrics do not prove diagnostic preservation.

evidenceLinks.claim: SAGE combines a large multi-crop image collection with source-grounded symptom knowledge and an agentic visual reasoning baseline.
evidenceLinks.limitation: SAGE is an adjacent agentic/VLM task and a non-archival workshop contribution; it is not directly comparable to closed-set calibrated classification.

evidenceLinks.claim: The CCMT data paper reports 24,881 raw Ghanaian crop images and a separate augmented collection of 102,976 images across 22 categories.
evidenceLinks.limitation: The data paper does not establish the source-level duplicate relationships or leakage in a chosen train/test split; audit the released files and keep augmented derivatives grouped with their originals.

evidenceLinks.claim: The Gookyi et al. dataset documents Ghanaian multi-modal field-trial observations and field photographs for cowpea and maize.
evidenceLinks.limitation: The published dataset description does not identify disease labels; it is contextual field data, not a disease-labelled test benchmark.

evidenceLinks.claim: The paper explicitly identifies evaluation across seasons, devices and geographic regions as needed beyond its single PaddyDoctor corpus.
evidenceLinks.limitation: This is a limitation stated by one study, not proof that no other study has performed external validation.

evidenceLinks.claim: PALM-Net evaluates multiple named datasets and reports field-robustness claims, showing that multi-dataset evaluation is already part of the literature.
evidenceLinks.limitation: The available abstract does not establish that its protocol measures cross-domain calibration or selective risk.

evidenceLinks.claim: EffiToRag provides a recent held-out benchmark and a knowledge-grounded diagnostic pipeline.
evidenceLinks.limitation: The available abstract does not establish calibration transfer across independent geographic/acquisition domains.

evidenceLinks.claim: SAGE provides an adjacent agentic diagnosis approach with source-grounded symptom knowledge and a large multi-crop resource.
evidenceLinks.limitation: Its task and evaluation are not directly equivalent to calibrated classifier confidence and selective prediction.
